key_insight: Most of the LLM-generated clinical corpus was not new information: only 10.9% was trainable-unique content, while 79.4% was redundant.
clinical_relevance: For clinical AI training, raw corpus size can be misleading because duplicated or copied text can skew what models learn and reduce downstream performance.
method: Analyzed the full output of a multi-agent clinical extraction pipeline over 167,034 patient narratives.
Introduced provenance-based redundancy decomposition to classify every token by source.
Validated redundancy patterns with model-free lossless compression analysis.
evidence_signal: At production scale, 2.51 billion generated tokens were assessed, and de-duplicating the corpus improved a clinical encoder on external disease-recognition benchmarks at equal token budget.
watch_item: Some redundancy is losslessly removable, but duplicated generated text across records is not; implementation needs careful channel-specific handling to avoid discarding useful signal.
paper_title: How much of an LLM-generated clinical corpus is actually new? A production-scale measurement of content redundancy for provenance classification
